Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event
The same time of day the event occurred

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: A medical-equipment visual trigger is hard to reconcile as a central combat-related trigger for this profile, especially alongside otherwise combat-consistent threat items and without any medical/hospital-related memory or appraisal content. It suggests a different trauma context and is clinically difficult to integrate with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall + Emotionless Recall + Memory Feels Alien
issues.explanation: Within Memory, intense rage on recall conflicts with the paired reports of emotionally numb recall and the memory feeling alien/detached. Fluctuation can occur, but as a compact three-item profile these items pull in opposing directions—high emotional arousal versus marked dissociative detachment—without other memory content to bridge them.

Memory: Rage on Recall + Emotionless Recall + Memory Feels Alien

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Rage on Recall' conflicts with the paired endorsement of markedly detached recall ('Emotionless Recall' and 'Memory Feels Alien'). Intense rage during recall and recall experienced as numb/alien can both occur in PTSD, but selecting all three as coequal memory descriptors creates a direct within-node tension between highly affect-laden remembering and strongly depersonalized, affectless remembering. The rest of the profile coherently reflects severe combat-related PTSD, but this specific Memory combination is the main clinically questionable inconsistency.

issues.item: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, two items describe markedly detached/derealized recall ('emotionless', 'belongs to someone else') while another describes intensely affect-laden reliving ('same terror I felt at the time'). These can both occur across different moments in PTSD, but as the only three selected memory items they pull in opposing directions and are not a clean, internally coherent depiction of a single dominant memory style for this profile.

These two appraisals are plausible in severe PTSD, but for a 63-year-old married airline pilot they create a hard-to-explain mismatch with the rest of the profile when presented without any trauma-linked appraisal content. 'I have no future' is especially discordant for an older, still-employed patient and is not well integrated with the combat-specific trigger/threat pattern. The Negative Appraisals node is dominated by global depressive identity/future statements rather than trauma-related meanings that would plausibly connect to the very strong Triggers → Negative Appraisals edge in the formulation.

vignette: John, a 63-year-old airline pilot of Oceania descent, has been haunted by his combat experiences for years. During a mission in Afghanistan, he was involved in an intense firefight while on a helicopter reconnaissance mission at dusk. The tactile memory of the rough sand and the constant whirring noise of the helicopters' rotors have become potent triggers for John. Every time he feels a similar texture or hears a sound reminiscent of those moments, he is instantly transported back to that terrifying experience. John's night vigilance is particularly pronounced; the darkness seems to amplify his sense of vulnerability. Each evening, as twilight begins to fall, he finds it increasingly difficult to feel safe. The same time of day when the traumatic event occurred intensifies his anxiety, making him hyper-aware and on edge. Even at home with his wife, he scans the room continuously for exits and remains vigilant about sudden movements by others, always ready to react defensively. His memories of that fateful mission are fragmented and feel alien to him. Despite being a key participant in those events, John often struggles to integrate these memories into his sense of self. When triggered, these memories return with a terrifying force, reenacting the intense fear he felt at the time. The sudden recall is often precipitated by an auditory cue or a particular texture, leaving him feeling disoriented and overwhelmed. John's negative appraisals have significantly impacted his outlook on life and himself. He harbors deep-seated beliefs that there is something fundamentally wrong with him as a person. This self-perception has eroded much of the joy he once found in life. What was once filled with happiness now feels perpetually dark and miserable. The constant vigilance and fear have made it difficult for John to engage fully with his work or his relationships, including that with his wife. Over time, these avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on both his professional and personal life. He has become increasingly isolated at home, avoiding social gatherings and family outings where the risk of being exposed to triggers is high. His job as an airline pilot requires him to be in constant proximity to aircraft sounds, making each day a potential trigger for his symptoms. John's colleagues have noticed changes in his demeanor; he appears more distant and preoccupied. John has also begun to avoid certain aspects of his daily routine. For instance, he no longer walks the familiar paths near his home that are lined with sand-like textures reminiscent of the desert sands where his traumatic experiences took place. This avoidance has gradually isolated him from activities he once enjoyed, leaving him feeling more disconnected from both his work and personal life. The cumulative impact of these symptoms finally pushed John to seek help after a particularly distressing episode at work. During a routine flight, the sound of another helicopter passing overhead triggered a full relapse of his traumatic memories. He experienced such intense fear that he was unable to focus on flying safely for several minutes, leading to a near-miss incident that could have had catastrophic consequences. This close call was a wake-up call for John. He realized that his condition is not only affecting him but also putting others at risk. What frightens him most is the thought of losing control again in such critical situations and endangering lives. At the same time, he is hopeful that with professional help, he can regain some measure of peace and stability. John's journey to seek help reflects a deep-seated fear of being permanently damaged by his experiences but also a glimmer of hope for recovery. He hopes to reclaim parts of his life that have been lost to the constant vigilance and terror that now dominate his existence.
